original: For professors, publishing in elite journals is an unavoidable part of university life. The grueling process of subjecting work to the up-or-down judgment of credentialed scholarly peers has been a cornerstone of academic culture since at least the mid-20
sampled:
th century. But it’s increasingly difficult to make it to the top journals in the humanities and social sciences (HSS). Indeed, the majority of humanities scholars and social scientists do not publish in any journals at all. So why go through the time, effort and cost of publishing, especially for people whose work may not be getting published?

Because elite journals are a competitive market. Measure 97 was failing 58 percent to 42 percent as of 9:50 p.m.

ought campaign in which opponents claimed that the initiative would disproportionately hit low-income communities, would do little to stimulate economic growth and could be used to enact a cash-for-clunkers program.
The Yes on 97 campaign had raised more than $40 million, largely through contributions from the Microsoft Corp. and the Service Employees International Union. The opposition group was outspent, particularly in the final weeks of the campaign.
"It was a close race, but our campaign worked tirelessly to educate voters," said Jim Campbell, a spokesman for Yes on 97.
